newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE-El Dorado scramble is ecologists' road to hell.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-El Dorado scramble is ecologists' road to hell.

text.p: Gold fever is bubbling in Venezuela's Imataca forest reserve, but to some the precious metal paves the road to hell.

Fly over southeastern Venezuela and it looks as though its vast forests have caught a skin disease: flaking white and red blotches where the earth has been sucked and sifted for gold. Zoom in and the eye picks out hillsides blasted treeless by high-pressure water hoses, rough shacks with black plastic roofs and hand-dug mine shafts dotting the ruined landscape.

Government officials say a recent decree to expand mining in Bolivar state will stop an area twice the size of Belgium from becoming an ecologically ruined badland of Dodge City shoot-outs, prostitution and disease. "There's no effective army presence, let alone environmental monitoring" as of now, government mining adviser Americo Martin said.

Not everyone agrees. Environmentalists argue the decree will accelerate the ruin of a unique and delicate ecosystem, one of the ten most diverse in the world. "The government admits it can't control the mining there already ... so why do they want to open more mines?" asked Ana Ponte, who heads the umbrella environmental group Coalicion Orinoquia-Amazonica.

Both sides have wrapped themselves in the environmental flag. The government says granting property rights will bring some of Bolivar state's 50,000 wildcat miners back within the law, allow for tighter environmental scrutiny and capture lost taxes on around 35 tonnes of gold mined illegally each year.

"Now Venezuela can count on an environmental mining policy that guarantees sustainable development," says an Environment Ministry notice widely published in national newspapers after hundreds of protesting Pemon Indians marched on Congress.
'MINING IS NOT ECOLOGICAL'

"Mining, basically, is not ecological," countered Ponte. The Guri dam, which powers more than two-thirds of the country, is already gummed-up by thousands of tonnes of sediment leached from small mines worked since 1989, she said.

In his Planning Ministry office in Caracas, Martin stooped over a U.S government geological survey of the area -- nothing less than a modern-day treasure map. "I don't understand people who would rather shed a tear over a felled tree than a man's prosperity or his life," he said.
Government figures show eight out of ten Venezuelans live in poverty.

"Look," Martin said, pointing to a dense cluster of geological symbols in the bottom right-hand corner. "Sir Walter Raleigh was right, El Dorado still exists!" The English explorer travelled up the Orinoco river 400 years ago in his failed quest for a legendary city of gold.

Venezuela may contain five to ten percent of the world's gold and miners are rubbing their hands at the prospect of exploring another 2.5 million acres (1 million hectares) under the decree. But opposition leaders complain there was no consultation over the law and environmental and Indian groups are seeking a blocking order from the Supreme Court.

With registered gold production tipped to rise within five years from 12 tonnes to 50 tonnes per year, allegations fly that government officials have a personal financial stake in the plan's successful implementation.
ENVIRONMENTAL RECORD BODES ILL FOR THE FUTURE
"The shame is Venezuela has beautiful nature, indigenous groups and massive mineral resources, but hitherto it's messed them all up on a broad front," a Western diplomat said.

At the end of the last century, Venezuela was the world's largest gold producer with around 17 tonnes per year. But oil overshadowed mining and the state-owned industry now counts on the world's largest reserves outside the Middle East.

Environmentalists fear that after despoiling western Venezuela with oil, the government wants to do the same in the east, with environmental rules treated much like Caracas traffic lights: to be ignored with little fear of reprisal.

Far from curbing uncontrolled mining, environmentalists argue the decree will lead to more access roads, encouraging an even greater influx of prospectors, including from neighbouring Brazil, Guyana and Colombia.
"What do people want? That the Virgin Mary comes down to Venezuela? I reject such pessimism. Venezuela can successfully administer itself," Martin fumed.

But everyone admits environmental management of the reserve is poor and ecological damage is already catching up. Heavy trucks laden with timber regularly use the single good road that cuts north through the forest, weighed down with the fruit of unsupervised but legal "managed logging."
'NEVER SEEN A TRUCK WITH SEEDLINGS'

"I've seen those trucks all my life," said Eduardo Cartaya, who grew up in Bolivar state and now works as a social programme manager for Canadian mining company Placer Dome. "But I've never seen one carrying seedlings."
Foreign investment is the government's clinching argument for the decree, with transnationals seen boosting employment while weaning miners off the mercury used to process gold ore.

The government hopes to break the bureaucratic log-jam that has all but killed off a 1990s gold opening. Seventy companies rushed in at first. Now only a handful remain, their mining applications lost in Venezuela's byzantine legal maze.

In the south of the reserve at the Las Cristinas joint venture mine, grassy plots reveal environmental recovery tests where top-soil has been removed, replaced and re-seeded with local species. "Full recovery clearly takes a long time but it's very do-able," Cartaya said.

The company lets small miners work some of the grounds in a part social project, part escape valve for locals who might otherwise invade the mine. Government ministers have embraced Placer's carefully nurtured scheme as a forerunner of ecologically sound mining and the kind of big business/small miner cooperation they envisage throughout the reserve.
